title: The 76 Refrigerators Zhang Ruimin Would Not Sell
dek: In 1985 the new director of a failing Qingdao fridge factory had 76 faulty units smashed instead of sold off cheaply as seconds.

story.event: Having 76 faulty refrigerators smashed instead of sold as seconds
story.summary: In 1985 Zhang Ruimin, put in charge of a near-bankrupt city-owned refrigerator factory in Qingdao the year before, found 76 defective refrigerators among about 400 in stock and had them smashed with sledgehammers rather than sold cheaply; by his own account the workers responsible broke their own units and he swung first. The plant was profitable by 1986, won a national quality gold medal in December 1988 and grew into Haier.
paragraphs: In 1984 the city of Qingdao moved Zhang Ruimin, then 35 and an official in its appliance administration, to run a refrigerator factory that was failing. By one company history it could not pay its roughly 600 workers and struggled to make 80 refrigerators a month. Zhang later said his first rule was that nobody could urinate on the factory floor, and that he could not fire anyone who did; workers then could not be dismissed. The factory had bought refrigerator technology from Germany's Liebherr, and Zhang said his visits there, where everything was standardised, shaped what came next.

In 1985, in the fullest accounts, a customer brought back a refrigerator that did not work. Checking the stock of about 400 finished units for a good one, Zhang found that nearly one in five had failed inspection: 76 refrigerators. The usual course was to sell faulty units cheaply as seconds, and they were not cheap to lose. "Back then a refrigerator cost the equivalent of two years' wages for a worker," he said in 2016.

He had them lined up and destroyed. In that 2016 interview he said a note on each one named its fault and the person responsible, who then had to smash it, and that he swung the first sledgehammer himself. "Some workers wept, but it proved a useful exercise." Retellings differ. A 2001 Wharton report of a talk he gave has Zhang smashing all 76 alone; TIME in 2014 had workers handed hammers and Zhang breaking one. Haier's own timeline speaks of complaint letters rather than a single customer. Nearly everything about the scene comes from Zhang and his company, and the Irish Times began its 2019 telling with "legend has it". The same paper reported that the story got Zhang into trouble with the authorities at the time.

What followed is easier to check. By 1986, according to the company history, the plant was profitable. In a national refrigerator appraisal in December 1988 it scored highest and won what Haier calls the first gold medal in the history of Chinese refrigerators. The factory became Haier, which by 2014 employed about 70,000 people. One of the sledgehammers is in the permanent collection of the National Museum of China.

quote.text: For there is a shame that bringeth sin; and there is a shame that is glory and grace.
quote.work: Ecclesiasticus (The Wisdom of Ben Sira) and the Wisdom of Solomon
quote.source_title: The Wisdom of the Apocrypha, Project Gutenberg eBook #77250
quote.connection: Ben Sira separates the shame that pushes people towards wrongdoing from the shame that is a kind of honour. Zhang put a name on every faulty refrigerator, and some of those named wept. Which kind each of them carried away from that floor, no account tells us.

reflection: Throwing away work that is nearly good enough has a cost, and Zhang made sure everyone could see it. The refrigerators were worth years of wages; that is why the morning was remembered, and perhaps why it worked.

You will meet smaller versions of it: a batch that fails a check, a report you know is thin, a piece of a colleague's work that is not ready. Refusing to pass it on is one decision. How you speak to the person whose name is on it is another, and they will remember that one longer. Naming a fault plainly, without making a show of the maker, is quieter than a sledgehammer and harder to do well.
invitation: Think of one piece of work this week that is nearly good enough. Decide today whether it goes out. If it does not, tell the person who made it what is wrong in one plain sentence, in private.

sources.title: Business leader Zhang Ruimin on the importance of change for companies (Think:Act, "Vigilant" issue)
sources.publisher: Roland Berger, Think:Act Magazine (Henrik Bork, 13 December 2016)
sources.supports: Zhang's own account: 1985, a year after he became director; 76 faulty refrigerators smashed; workers could not be dismissed; his trips to Germany and visit to Liebherr, where everything was standardised; 'Back then a refrigerator cost the equivalent of two years' wages for a worker'; a note on each refrigerator naming the quality problem and the person responsible, who had to smash it; 'Some workers wept, but it proved a useful exercise'; he was the first to wield the sledgehammer; took over the plant in 1984.

sources.title: This CEO Wants to Hold Chinese Products to a Haier Standard
sources.publisher: Knowledge at Wharton, University of Pennsylvania (11 April 2001)
sources.supports: Report of Zhang's talk at Wharton: appointed in 1984 at 35 by the Qingdao municipal government's household appliance division; the factory suffering great losses; his first rule against urinating on the floor and his inability to fire anyone ('You couldn't be fired'); 76 refrigerators found outmoded, incomplete or otherwise defective; this account has Zhang smashing all 76 himself; later sales in Shanghai.

sources.title: Zhang Ruimin's Haier Power
sources.supports: City government put Zhang in charge of a dysfunctional, near-bankrupt refrigerator maker; workers urinating on the floor; in 1985 a customer returned a faulty fridge and Zhang found many others broken in inventory; 76 flawed appliances lined up, workers handed sledgehammers and Zhang smashing one; one sledgehammer in the Haier showroom and another in the permanent collection of China's National Museum; about 70,000 employees in 2014.

sources.title: How Haier morphed from tiny operation into global corporation
sources.supports: Introduces the episode with 'legend has it'; 76 substandard units; the alternative of selling them cheaply as seconds; Zhang smashing some and the workers who made them finishing the job; Zhang's explanation about personal responsibility; the story spreading and landing Zhang in trouble with the authorities at the time; the highest accolade for quality in China by 1988; the shop-floor toilet rule.

sources.title: Haier Group Corporation (International Directory of Company Histories)
sources.supports: Factory unable to pay its 600 workers and close to bankruptcy; output struggling to top 80 refrigerators a month; Liebherr's refrigerator technology sold to the factory with the city of Qingdao's agreement; a customer's return, the check of about 400 finished refrigerators of which nearly 20 per cent had failed inspection; 76 units lined up and smashed with sledgehammers; the plant profitable by 1986; the later name Haier taken from the Chinese rendering of Liebherr.

sources.title: Haier History
sources.supports: Haier's own telling: consumer letters complaining of quality in 1985 and Zhang breaking 76 substandard refrigerators to raise quality awareness, 'the warning bell of quality'; in the National Refrigerators Appraisal of December 1988 Haier scored highest and won the first gold medal in China's refrigerator history.

cross_checks.claim: In 1985 Zhang had 76 defective refrigerators smashed with sledgehammers.
When Zhang took over in 1984 the factory was close to bankruptcy.
Zhang's first rule banned urinating on the factory floor, and he could not fire workers.
The episode began with a customer returning a faulty refrigerator and a check of the stock.
Zhang himself swung a sledgehammer, and the workers who made the faulty units smashed them.

research_notes: The scene rests almost entirely on Zhang's and Haier's own telling; no contemporary 1985 report was found, and the Irish Times (2019) introduces it with 'legend has it'. The story attributes accordingly. The number 76 is the same in every account (Zhang 2016, Wharton 2001, TIME 2014, Irish Times 2019, Gale's company history, Haier's timeline), and the company history's 'nearly 20 per cent' of about 400 units fits it. Who swung the hammers differs: Zhang (Roland Berger 2016) says the person named on each unit smashed it and he swung first; TIME (2014) says workers were handed hammers and Zhang smashed one; the Irish Times says he smashed some and the workers finished; Knowledge at Wharton (2001, summarising his talk) says he smashed all 76 himself. The story gives Zhang's own account and names the Wharton and TIME versions. The trigger also differs: a single customer's return (TIME, Gale history) or complaint letters (Haier timeline); Wharton mentions only an inventory check. The 'two years' wages' value is Zhang's own claim and is quoted as such; no source gives a price or wage figure. Worker count (600) and output (under 80 a month) come only from the Gale history and are introduced as 'by one company history'. Funding is 'public': the factory was owned by the city of Qingdao (Gale history) and Zhang was appointed by the municipal government (Wharton, TIME). TIME's article is also reprinted on haier.com; the TIME original is cited. The National Museum detail comes from TIME alone. The Ben Sira verse is from the Revised Version text in the Wisdom of the East selection; it is Ecclesiasticus 4:21.
